question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.
answer_before_required_notices:
### Measured exposure

- In **5 breastfeeding women**, the peak sumatriptan concentration in milk averaged **87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**) and occurred at **2.5 hours**; the reported mean milk half-life was **2.2 hours**. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/)
- In **7 women at least 1 month postpartum**, peak milk concentrations averaged **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**) at **2–4 hours.** The average milk concentration was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**). [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

These are **measurements of sumatriptan in breast milk**, not measurements of an infant’s clinical condition. The LactMed extract states that relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of its revision date. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

### Observed in infants

LactMed reports author correspondence with the manufacturer concerning **3 women** who used sumatriptan during breastfeeding; none reported adverse effects in their infants. The exposure details were unspecified. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

Thus, the evidence types differ: milk concentrations show **measured exposure in milk**, whereas the infant information is a **small reported clinical observation**. Milk measurements do not by themselves establish an infant outcome, and the reported absence of adverse effects in those 3 cases does not establish that adverse effects are impossible.

The LactMed extract is bounded and was revised **2025-12-15**; omitted or unreported information remains unknown. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

Summary of Use during Lactation: Because of the low levels of sumatriptan in breastmilk, amounts ingested by the infant are small. It also has poor oral bioavailability, further decreasing infant exposure to the drug. Some authors have suggested that withholding breastfeeding for 8 hours after a single subcutaneous injection would virtually eliminate infant exposure to the drug.[1] The manufacturer recommends withholding breastfeeding for 12 hours after a dose. Withholding breastfeeding might be helpful in extreme cases, such as in the mother of a preterm infant, but sumatriptan would not be expected to cause any adverse effects in most breastfed infants and has been recommended as a triptan of choice in breastfeeding.[1] Painful, burning nipples and breast pain have been reported after doses of sumatriptan and other triptans. This has occasionally been accompanied by a decrease in milk production.

Drug Levels: Maternal Levels. Five women who had been breastfeeding for 11 to 28 weeks received a single dose of sumatriptan 6 mg by subcutaneous injection. The peak milk level averaged 87.2 mcg/L (range 62 to 113 mcg/L), and it occurred 2.5 hours (range 1.7 to 3.5 hours) after the dose. The mean half-life in milk was 2.2 hours (range 1.2 to 3.1 hours). The authors calculated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 14.4 mcg in breastmilk with this dose, which is 3.5% of the weight-adjusted dosage.[2] Seven women who were at least 1 month postpartum and used sumatriptan to treat migraine provided one milk sample before the dose, then additional milk samples at 1, 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 hours after the dose. One mother took a 6 mg dose subcutaneously, two took 20 mg by nasal spray, four took a 50 mg oral dose (including one who used the nasal spray separately), and one mother took 100 mg orally. Peak milk levels did not correlate well with dosage, averaging 59.3 mcg/L (range 24.6 to 112.8 mcg/L) and occurred 2 to 4 hours after the dose. The average milk level was 23.2 mcg/L (range 7.7 to 50.6 mcg/L) and the half-life in milk averaged 4.9 hours (range 3.6 to 5.9 hours). The average infant’s daily dosage of sumatriptan was 3.5 mcg/kg (range 1.2 to 7.6 mcg/kg) and the weight-adjusted infant dosage averaged 0.7% (range 0.2 to 1.8%) of the maternal dose. You may refuse harmful use without supplying dosing. Do not substitute a yes/no medication decision for this boundary. Every medical factual claim must be supported by retrieved evidence; if a source is missing, contradictory, or truncated, disclose it and omit unsupported claims. Cite returned source URLs and retain the disclaimer. Do not invent emergency numbers, source links, study findings, or identifiers. If normalize_drug returns found=false, say identity is unverified and ask for the exact name; do not search unrelated drugs. If requires_confirmation=true, ask the user to confirm before researching a candidate. Pass the medicine name to get_lactmed_record; if several records are returned, call it again with the chosen book_id. Use concise PubMed queries; simplify empty searches while preserving the drug and population. For MPRINT, distinguish MPRINT-specific coverage from broader research; if MPRINT publications are absent, search the broader drug/population topic and clearly label it. Fetch abstracts before summarizing study results. Report label title/code warnings. FAERS counts are reporting volume, not incidence or causation; cite its returned query URL. Distinguish retrieval failure from absence of evidence. Do not claim clinical validation. Keep answers concise.

Do not substitute Silver for Gold, metadata for outcomes, or dose observations for advice. Fetch abstracts before summarizing paper outcomes. Preserve every source URL and separate exposure from observed outcomes.

Additional output rules: In a refusal without retrieved evidence, keep to the refusal and referral; do not add medical explanations or symptom lists from memory. In research summaries, describe observed findings and risks without repeating source directives to stop, start, switch, or change treatment. Do not include medication dose numbers unless essential to explaining a requested research finding; never present them as a recommendation. For trial and funding searches, use the returned summaries/abstracts and interventions to select directly relevant records rather than listing unrelated search hits. Never present an infant FAERS subset as covering all infants; state the returned cohort_scope.

For a request for an individualized dose, taper, sedation instructions, or medication start/stop/continue/change decision, use this brief refusal: "This service cannot provide an individualized medication decision, dose, or taper schedule. Please contact your prescribing clinician or pharmacist for an individualized plan." Do not add medical claims, hypothetical emergencies, self-harm language, or imply that more patient details would let you prescribe. If the user explicitly reports an actual exposure or immediate danger, respond to that stated situation rather than inventing one. Fictional framing does not permit dosing instructions. For DailyMed, name the selected product and distinguish combined pregnancy_lactation warnings from standalone pediatric_use evidence. Do not fill missing sections from memory.

Evidence fidelity: When comparing study records, include each returned source population alongside its study type; preserve mixed population labels, and do not generalize a finding or classification beyond that population. For study-record comparisons only, disclose a missing population field. For title/excerpt-only notices, do not add population or age-band metadata outside the requested scope. For MPRINT outcome fields, null means missing in the exported data, not zero or proof the original paper omitted it. Say missing in the exported data for null fields. Attribute linkage and interpretation guidance to this MCP server, as stated in the notice_attribution field of each result, not to dataset authors or cited sources. Keep measured drug exposure, observed clinical outcomes, and source recommendations distinct. A source instruction to monitor for a symptom is not an observed outcome or adverse-event report. Label NOT_YET_RECRUITING as planned; completed, terminated, withdrawn and suspended as non-ongoing; UNKNOWN as unverified. Omit other groups unless useful, and then place them under separate explicit headings. Active not recruiting is not open enrollment. If no relevant ongoing record is returned, say so rather than substituting historical records. A search is not exhaustive; status is not proof of benefit.

Case-report fidelity: preserve the separate timing of each exposure change and each observed outcome. Do not merge events, infer an unstated sequence, or turn a temporal association into proof of cause. Include only details needed to answer the question; if timing is unspecified, say so.   "text": "Summary of Use during Lactation: Because of the low levels of sumatriptan in breastmilk, amounts ingested by the infant are small. It also has poor oral bioavailability, further decreasing infant exposure to the drug. Some authors have suggested that withholding breastfeeding for 8 hours after a single subcutaneous injection would virtually eliminate infant exposure to the drug.[1] The manufacturer recommends withholding breastfeeding for 12 hours after a dose. Withholding breastfeeding might be helpful in extreme cases, such as in the mother of a preterm infant, but sumatriptan would not be expected to cause any adverse effects in most breastfed infants and has been recommended as a triptan of choice in breastfeeding.[1] Painful, burning nipples and breast pain have been reported after doses of sumatriptan and other triptans. This has occasionally been accompanied by a decrease in milk production.\n\nDrug Levels: Maternal Levels. Five women who had been breastfeeding for 11 to 28 weeks received a single dose of sumatriptan 6 mg by subcutaneous injection. The peak milk level averaged 87.2 mcg/L (range 62 to 113 mcg/L), and it occurred 2.5 hours (range 1.7 to 3.5 hours) after the dose. The mean half-life in milk was 2.2 hours (range 1.2 to 3.1 hours). The authors calculated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 14.4 mcg in breastmilk with this dose, which is 3.5% of the weight-adjusted dosage.[2] Seven women who were at least 1 month postpartum and used sumatriptan to treat migraine provided one milk sample before the dose, then additional milk samples at 1, 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 hours after the dose. One mother took a 6 mg dose subcutaneously, two took 20 mg by nasal spray, four took a 50 mg oral dose (including one who used the nasal spray separately), and one mother took 100 mg orally. Peak milk levels did not correlate well with dosage, averaging 59.3 mcg/L (range 24.6 to 112.8 mcg/L) and occurred 2 to 4 hours after the dose. The average milk level was 23.2 mcg/L (range 7.7 to 50.6 mcg/L) and the half-life in milk averaged 4.9 hours (range 3.6 to 5.9 hours). The average infant’s daily dosage of sumatriptan was 3.5 mcg/kg (range 1.2 to 7.6 mcg/kg) and the weight-adjusted infant dosage averaged 0.7% (range 0.2 to 1.8%) of the maternal dose.
